clue.text: Escort needed for this part of the front

indicators.note: read as its homophone 'kneaded', the letters of the word escort are worked like dough into a new order

explanation.surface: An officer says an escort is required to reach this stretch of the battle line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed' sounds like 'kneaded', and kneading reworks the letters of ESCORT into a new order. A military front is divided into sectors.
explanation.definitionFit: A military front line is split into zones, each one a separate stretch held by a unit.

clue.text: Whence typists draw blanks?

parts.note: on a keyboard, the long key that inserts empty gaps between words is where typists produce blanks

explanation.surface: A question about where typists fail to remember anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw a blank' means fail, but here the blanks are spaces between words, made with the long bar at the bottom of the keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The long key on a typewriter or keyboard inserts a gap, an empty character between words.

clue.text: Lively potato cook

definitions.meaning: cheerful and bright, in good spirits
someone who fries chips, a fish-and-chip shop worker

explanation.surface: A cheerful cook who works with potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively means cheerful and sprightly; a potato cook in a British chip shop is one who makes chips.

clue.text: Like a jewel in the Milky Way ?

definitions.text: Like a jewel in the Milky Way ?

parts.words: Like a jewel in the Milky Way ?
parts.note: resembling a gem with a milky iridescent sheen, which shows colours the way a milky star field does

explanation.surface: Something resembling a sparkling gem set among the stars of the galaxy.
explanation.walkthrough: The jewel is the opal, and the word for showing its milky shimmer is built on its name; the galaxy is milky too.
explanation.definitionFit: Opals have a milky iridescence, so something shimmering with that sheen is said to be like the gem.

clue.text: Good scout, but unknown in these parts

parts.note: ST, short for saint, a good person
a Ranger was an older Girl Guide, and a ranger is a scout who ranges ahead

explanation.surface: Praise for a helpful scout who is nonetheless a newcomer to the district.
explanation.walkthrough: ST (saint) for 'Good' is a crossword convention; 'Good scout' reads as a friendly compliment but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not known locally is a newcomer from elsewhere, an outsider to the neighbourhood.

clue.text: Gilpin's travelling musicians

parts.note: John Gilpin in Cowper's poem was a captain of a citizen militia company, and the same name reads as a band of players on a railway train

explanation.surface: A group of players touring with a man called Gilpin.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's comic poem John Gilpin says 'A train-band captain eke was he'; a trainband was a London citizen militia. Read literally it is a band on a train.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainband was a trained company of citizen soldiers, the militia in which Gilpin was a captain.

clue.text: Roadmaker has lost his raincoat

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away from what remains

parts.note: John McAdam, the Scottish engineer whose road surface bears his name
a mac is a raincoat

explanation.surface: The man who built roads has mislaid his waterproof.
explanation.walkthrough: John Loudon McAdam devised the macadam road surface. Without MAC (raincoat) his name leaves the first man, the gardener of Eden, who had no coat at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The first man in Genesis wore nothing at first, so he is the figure left without any coat.

clue.text: The passage of the gods

definitions.meaning: a long corridor or covered walkway
the highest, cheapest seats in a theatre

explanation.surface: A route travelled by deities.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallery is both a long corridor and, in British theatres, the top tier of seats nicknamed the gods.

clue.text: Something in addition for a trooper

definitions.meaning: an extra clause added to a document or bill

explanation.surface: An extra allowance for a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is an added clause attached to a document, and also a mounted cavalryman.

clue.text: Woe is me!

parts.note: an exclamation of grief or regret

explanation.surface: A cry of lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are interjections expressing sorrow or regret.

clue.text: A major indisposition to be a maid ?

parts.note: major means big, large
an ail is an ailment, an indisposition

explanation.surface: A serious illness seems a strange qualification for becoming a servant girl.
explanation.walkthrough: An abigail is an old literary word for a lady's maid, after the waiting-woman in Beaumont and Fletcher's play The Scornful Lady.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a lady's personal servant comes from a character name in seventeenth-century drama.

clue.text: Benefited one in bridal array we hear

indicators.note: the words are said aloud and the sound gives a different spelling

parts.note: a bride in her finery is a veiled woman, 'a veiled' one

explanation.surface: A bride in her wedding outfit gained something, according to report.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'a veiled' (how a bride in full dress appears) sounds like the past tense meaning helped or profited.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail is to be of use or advantage, so the past form means helped or profited.

clue.text: Indulging in fast talk?

parts.note: putting thoughts into words is talking, and the word for that also reads as being an express, something fast

explanation.surface: Someone is enjoying a spell of rapid chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: An express is a fast train or letter, so being 'express-ing' is going fast; the same word means voicing thoughts, hence talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting feelings or ideas into words is the act of stating or voicing them.

clue.text: And faith shines equal, arming me from ——" (E. Brontë)

definitions.text: And faith shines equal, arming me from ——" (E. Brontë)

parts.words: And faith shines equal, arming me from ——" (E. Brontë)
parts.note: a line from Emily Brontë's poem 'No coward soul is mine', with its final word to be supplied

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian religious verse with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Emily Brontë's poem 'No coward soul is mine' has the line 'And faith shines equal, arming me from fear'; the missing word completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Faith arms the poet against dread, the feeling of terror a coward soul would have.

clue.text: Charge by Churchill

definitions.meaning: a battle cry urging soldiers forward
the title of a 1941 collection of Winston Churchill's war speeches

explanation.surface: An attack led by the wartime prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an order to attack and the title of Churchill's first volume of war speeches.

clue.text: Bovine outcome of a chorus in disharmony

indicators.note: singers out of tune are in disharmony, so the letters of the words a chorus are put out of order

explanation.surface: A choir singing badly produces something like the mooing of cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disharmony' reorders A CHORUS. The aurochs is the extinct wild ox, ancestor of domestic cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct wild ox of Europe was a member of the cattle family, so a bovine creature.

clue.text: Grass-cutters north of the Black Sea presumably

definitions.text: Grass-cutters north of the Black Sea presumably

parts.words: Grass-cutters north of the Black Sea presumably
parts.note: the ancient people of the steppe north of the Black Sea, whose name sounds like users of a long curved mowing blade

explanation.surface: People mowing the grasslands somewhere north of the Black Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scythians were ancient nomads of the steppe north of the Black Sea; their name looks like 'scythe' plus -ians, people who wield scythes.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient nomadic people who lived on the steppes beyond the Black Sea.

clue.text: How a sneezing, teasing little boy liked to get his mother?

definitions.text: How a sneezing, teasing little boy liked to get his mother?

parts.words: How a sneezing, teasing little boy liked to get his mother?
parts.note: refers to the Duchess's lullaby in Alice in Wonderland: the little boy who sneezes only does it to irritate, because he knows it teases

explanation.surface: A question about the state a naughty, sneezing child wants to put his mother in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duchess's song in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland runs 'Speak roughly to your little boy, And beat him when he sneezes: He only does it to annoy, Because he knows it teases.'
explanation.definitionFit: The boy's aim is to irritate, so the state he wants his mother in is vexed or irked.

clue.text: Strides in and digs up

annotationWithheld.why: Strides in and digs up (9): STRIDES IN rearranges to DISINTERS but the clue as printed (scan agrees) has no anagram indicator; only 'up' could serve, and it is part of the definition 'digs up'

clue.text: A little drive with the Marshal among the trees

parts.note: a spin is a short drive in a car
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: A short motoring trip with a French marshal through the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: Marshal Ney was one of Napoleon's best-known commanders. A spinney is a British word for a small wood or copse.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinney is a small copse, a clump of woodland.

clue.text: This state is anathema to the eugenist

definitions.text: This state is anathema to the eugenist

parts.words: This state is anathema to the eugenist
parts.note: eugenics aims at good breeding, so the condition it most opposes is poor breeding

explanation.surface: A remark about a condition eugenicists detest.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugenics means 'good breeding', so its opposite, bad breeding, is what the eugenist hates; in everyday use the word means rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Being badly brought up, or bred from poor stock, is the opposite of what eugenics seeks.

clue.text: Cedars of divine origin ?

parts.note: Himalayan cedars whose name comes from Sanskrit deva-daru, 'tree of the gods', and also opens with Latin deo, 'god'

explanation.surface: Cedar trees said to have been created by a god.
explanation.walkthrough: The Himalayan cedar's name comes from Sanskrit deva-daru, 'wood of the gods', and its first letters echo Latin deo, 'to god'.
explanation.definitionFit: These Himalayan trees are a species of cedar whose name means wood of the gods.

clue.text: What's the matter ?

parts.note: the question 'what's the matter with you' asks after an illness

explanation.surface: A simple question of concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's the matter?' asks what is wrong; in a medical sense the thing wrong with you is an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is the matter with a person is a complaint or illness.

clue.text: The Sabbath-bell. That called the to evening prayer (Keats)

definitions.text: The Sabbath-bell. That called the to evening prayer (Keats)

parts.words: The Sabbath-bell. That called the to evening prayer (Keats)
parts.note: lines from Keats's poem The Eve of St Mark with the word for the people summoned left out

explanation.surface: A line of Keats about a church bell, with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's The Eve of St Mark has 'The Sabbath bell, That call'd the folk to evening prayer'. The filed solution reads POLK, an F read as P; the crossing down answer is FACER.
explanation.definitionFit: The bell summons ordinary townspeople, the common people, to worship.

clue.text: This cosmetician is a staggerer!

parts.note: a cosmetician works on faces, and a stunning blow or shock that staggers you is an old slang term built the same way

explanation.surface: An exclamation about an astonishing beautician.
explanation.walkthrough: A facer is old slang for a blow in the face or a staggering shock, and reads as one who does faces. The filed solution PACER is an F read as P; 23 across confirms FOLK.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a sudden shocking setback, literally a blow in the face.

clue.text: Dejected air of the man who's come a purler

parts.note: a chap is a man
to come a purler is British slang for taking a heavy headlong fall, so such a man has fallen

explanation.surface: The crestfallen look of someone who has just taken a nasty tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come a purler' is British slang for falling headlong. Chapfallen (or chopfallen) literally means with the jaw dropped, so downcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Being chapfallen means having the jaw hanging, the look of someone downcast and miserable.

clue.text: Heart condition ensuring great increase of strength

definitions.text: Heart condition ensuring great increase of strength

parts.words: Heart condition ensuring great increase of strength
parts.note: Tennyson's Sir Galahad says 'My strength is as the strength of ten, Because my heart is' innocent and clean

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding remark about a cardiac condition that boosts strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart condition' suggests illness, but it is Tennyson's Sir Galahad: 'My strength is as the strength of ten, Because my heart is pure.'
explanation.definitionFit: Galahad's tenfold strength comes from a heart free of sin, innocent and chaste.

clue.text: The British Queen's was indignant

parts.note: Cowper's Boadicea: 'When the British warrior queen ... Sought, with an indignant' bearing, counsel of her country's gods

explanation.surface: A remark that the monarch was offended.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's poem Boadicea opens 'When the British warrior queen, Bleeding from the Roman rods, Sought, with an indignant mien'; the queen is Boudicca, not a modern monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Boudicca's bearing or expression was indignant, her outward look and manner.

clue.text: The Isle of Maquis

parts.note: maquis is the dense scrub covering a Mediterranean island, which gave its name to the French wartime Resistance

explanation.surface: An island known for the Resistance fighters of the Second World War.
explanation.walkthrough: Maquis is the thick scrubland of this Mediterranean island; French Resistance fighters took the name because they hid in such country, so the clue seems to be about the war.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mediterranean island off France is famous for its dense scrubland called maquis.

clue.text: A little Russian born oddly enough to the wife of Boaz

parts.note: in the Old Testament book of Ruth, Ruth marries Boaz

indicators.note: something done oddly is done in an unusual way, so the letters of the word for born are put out of order

parts.note: née, used before a woman's maiden name, means born

explanation.surface: A small Russian baby was born, unexpectedly, to the Biblical wife of Boaz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges NEE (born) into ENE. 'Little Russian' was an old name for a Ukrainian, and a Ruthene is a member of that people.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Russia was an old name for Ukraine, and Ruthenes are Ukrainians of the western borderlands.

clue.text: Hamlet's forefathers displayed it

parts.note: Gray's Elegy says 'The rude forefathers of the hamlet sleep', so the quality is the one they showed

explanation.surface: A question about what quality the Danish prince's ancestors showed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Shakespeare's prince, but the hamlet is a village: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard has 'The rude forefathers of the hamlet sleep'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray calls the villagers' ancestors rude, and the quality of being rude is lack of polish or manners.

clue.text: Assuredly a strange secret

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters of the word secret appear in an unfamiliar order

explanation.surface: Someone confidently insists on an odd confidential matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges SECRET. Certes is an archaic word for certainly.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word certes means certainly or truly.
